verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal, and precedents P7, P3 and P4 each point to this rework as the preferred fix. Five fixable design points survive at level 2. The weightiest are what happens to the core stats file when the module is removed (replication-ondisk-1), whether pg_stat_statements.save = off still works (replication-ondisk-2), and the empty query column at the text cap (standards-compat-1). Confidence is medium because only 3 of 29 messages are visible and replication-ondisk-1 rests on reader behaviour not shown in the material.

brief.title: Store pg_stat_statements entries as custom cumulative statistics
brief.problem: pg_stat_statements does not scale under high concurrency. Every counter update takes a per-entry spinlock, and eviction at pg_stat_statements.max holds an exclusive LWLock that blocks all backends. Query text garbage collection rewrites the whole text file under that lock. Users with many cores or many distinct queries see lock convoys, and changing pg_stat_statements.max needs a restart.
brief.proposed_design: The v5/v6 series stores statement entries as a custom pgstat kind in its own dshash, with counters accumulated per backend and merged on flush. Eviction becomes least-recently-used at about pg_stat_statements.max, with a hard backstop that stops new entries when allocated entries reach twice the max. A final patch moves query texts from the external file into capped shared memory.
user_visible_surface: pg_stat_statements.max changes from server-start to PGC_SIGHUP and becomes a soft limit.
New GUC pg_stat_statements.query_text_memory caps shared memory for query texts; the default moved from 64MB to 4MB during the thread.
pg_stat_statements_info.dealloc now counts evicted entries, not eviction runs.
pg_stat_force_next_flush() flushes non-transactional counters immediately when called inside a transaction.
pgstat C API for extensions: own_hash kind option, pgstat_get_hash_for_kind(), and an option to release references after flush.
author_claims: From 32 vCPUs up, 0004 gives 1.3x to 5x upstream TPS, close to a server without pg_stat_statements.
Under extreme churn on 96 and 192 vCPUs, 0004 has 2.6x to 5.1x upstream TPS.
Some low-client datapoints show 0004 1% to 4% slower than upstream.
All popular statements are kept, and the backstop is never hit with the reference-release patch.
Keeping texts in memory costs about what reading the text file already costs at each view query.
brief.thread_state: Several infrastructure pieces are committed, and the in-transaction flush moved to its own thread, where reviewers asked for a flush-context flag and an explicit callback result. No reviewer has replied to v5/v6, and in-memory-only query texts drew doubts at PGConf.EU.
unclear: v5 says nothing on which new pg_stat_statements_info columns remain from earlier versions.
The material does not say what users see when query_text_memory is full: an empty query column, and for how long.
The proposal does not say how the backstop of twice the max, or at most 20,000 more, was chosen, or whether users can tune it.
Message #28 is truncated, so open item 2 and later open items are not visible.
There are no tests for 0002, and the tests in 0003 and 0004 are not yet reviewed by the author.
The material does not say how existing pg_stat_statements stat files upgrade across the version 1.14 change.
Renaming the wait event pg_stat_statements to pg_stat_statements_alloc would break monitoring that matches the old name.

prior_attempts.title: Cancel problems of query to pg_stat_statements
prior_attempts.quote: This patch is only a workaround for a larger problem: the PGSS text file does not and will never scale once it reaches a large size and once we have a high turnover rate of the PGSS entries due to different query IDs.
prior_attempts.reason: Andrey Borodin first noted that the lock held during the file read blocks interrupts anyway; v2 worked around that. Michael Paquier then rejected the patch as only a workaround for a larger problem: the on-disk PGSS query text file does not scale once it is large and entries turn over often. He pointed instead to a planned rework that would move pg_stat_statements onto the pgstats API as a custom stats kind, with the query texts held entirely in memory.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P7 patched cancellation of the query text file read. This proposal does the rework P7's reviewer asked for: a custom stats kind, and in the final patch query texts held in shared memory.

prior_attempts.title: Sampling in pg_stat_statements
prior_attempts.quote: Since at the moment these changes are not a priority, and it's more important to address [0] for pg_stat_statements, I'm marking this patch as "Returned with Feedback".
prior_attempts.reason: The author withdrew it as Returned with Feedback, stating that the change was not a priority and that integrating pg_stat_statements with central pgstats was more important. Before that, the patch had been marked ready for committer, but no committer took it up. Alena Rybakina had objected that random sampling can drop the queries that matter.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P4 cut spinlock contention by random sampling, which can drop queries that matter. This proposal keeps full counts and removes the per-entry spinlock through backend-local pending stats, the pgstats integration P4 deferred to.

prior_attempts.title: Sampling of queries in pg_stat_statements
prior_attempts.quote: FWIW, I'm not eager to integrate this proposal without looking at this exact argument in depth.
prior_attempts.reason: The visible messages do not say why the author withdrew the entry, one day after posting it. The only reservation came from Michael Paquier, who did not want to add sampling before studying the actual bottlenecks. He suggested moving pg_stat_statements into the central pgstats with the custom APIs, which would remove the query text file and shrink the hash key, but he did not plan that work for PG18.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P3 also sampled queries to lower overhead. Its only reservation pointed to moving pg_stat_statements into central pgstats with the custom APIs, which this proposal does.

prior_attempts.title: Replace spinlock with lwlock in pg_stat_statements
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P12 swapped the per-entry spinlock for an LWLock. This proposal removes per-entry locking on the execution path. No reason is recorded for P12.

prior_attempts.title: Flush some statistics within running transactions
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P9 proposed flushing statistics inside running transactions, as 0001 does. The thread moved 0001 to its own thread, where reviewers asked for a flush-context flag and an explicit callback result. No reason is recorded for P9.

objections.title: Removing pg_stat_statements could discard all cumulative statistics at restart
objections.failure_scenario: An operator drops pg_stat_statements from shared_preload_libraries and restarts the server. At startup the stats file holds entries of a kind that is no longer registered, and pgstat may reject the whole file. Relation stats such as dead tuple counts reset, and autovacuum then works without them until activity rebuilds them.
objections.argument: Today pg_stat_statements writes its own file, so removing it leaves core stats untouched. With 0003 its entries are a custom kind written by the core pgstat machinery. As far as I know, the stats file reader treats an unknown kind as corruption and resets everything. The proposal does not say whether that path changes. pg_stat_statements is the most widely loaded custom kind, so this rare case would become common.
objections.author_must_show: What happens to relation and other core stats on restart when the stats file holds pg_stat_statements entries but the module is no longer loaded?

critic.reasoning: As far as I know, the stats file reader discards the whole file when it meets an entry of an unregistered kind, so the scenario is real. The visible material does not say what happens after the module is removed.

objections.title: pg_stat_statements.save = off no longer stops entries being saved
objections.failure_scenario: A user sets pg_stat_statements.save = off so that statement statistics do not survive a restart. After a clean restart, the entries come back from the core stats file, while their query texts, which are auxiliary data, are not saved. The user then sees old counters, possibly with an empty query column.
objections.argument: Message #18 says that write_to_file is fixed when the kind is registered. So save = off stops only the auxiliary data from being written, and the entries are still written. Message #18 also lists a runtime override of write_to_file as missing infrastructure. Neither the v5 description in message #28 nor the committed pieces it lists mention that override.
objections.author_must_show: In v5/v6, does pg_stat_statements.save = off still prevent entries from being written and restored, and how do entries and query texts stay consistent after restart?

critic.reasoning: Message #18 names the runtime override of write_to_file as missing, and the commits listed in message #28 do not include it. Message #28 is truncated, so a later open item may cover it, but nothing visible does.

objections.title: In-memory query texts can leave the query column empty after upgrade
objections.failure_scenario: A site with long ORM-generated queries upgrades and keeps the 4MB query_text_memory default. Once the cap fills, new entries show an empty query column. Monitoring snapshots that join on query text record entries they cannot label, and staff find this only when they need the text during an incident.
objections.argument: Today every tracked entry has its text, because the external file has no cap. In message #9, 0004 makes texts memory-only with a default of 4MB, and message #28 says real-world texts are much larger than the benchmark texts. No reviewer has replied on this, and message #28 reports doubts from PGConf.EU. The material does not say what users see when the cap is reached, or for how long.
objections.author_must_show: What does the query column return when query_text_memory is full, and how does an existing user learn the cap was reached?

critic.reasoning: Message #9 partly answers it: the query column is empty, and the text is filled in when the entry is next touched after the cap is raised. The proposal does not say how a user learns the cap was reached, and message #28 leaves the 4MB default open.

objections.title: Release-after-flush option and stale-ref check fit only pg_stat_statements
objections.failure_scenario: A later pgstat change alters how entry references are counted or garbage-collected but tests only the default mode. Kinds that set the new release-at-flush option then keep dropped entries alive or free them early. pg_stat_statements hits its backstop and stops tracking new statements, and users find out from missing rows.
objections.argument: Message #28 introduces 0002 with no thread of its own and no tests, and it puts pgstat_entry_ref_is_stale() in pgstat_internal.h for one extension. Message #25 already objected that the series exposes dshash details to stats kinds and couples drop helpers to scan state. Reference lifetime then has two modes, and pgstat maintainers must keep both correct. Message #28 shows the 3.3 design depends on this option to stay below the backstop.
objections.author_must_show: Which other stats kind would use release-at-flush, and what test fails if a future pgstat change breaks it?

critic.reasoning: Message #28 names no second user for release-at-flush and confirms 0002 has no thread of its own yet. Message #25 was about pgstat_drop_current() in v4 and must not be used as support here.

objections.title: dealloc keeps its name but changes its meaning
objections.failure_scenario: A monitoring tool alerts on the rate of pg_stat_statements_info.dealloc, which until now counted eviction runs. After upgrade the same column counts evicted entries, which can be hundreds per run. Alerts fire or thresholds drift with no change in workload, and operators find the cause only by reading the release notes.
objections.argument: Message #9 states the change in semantics and asks for other views, and no one replied. The documentation hunk redefines the column in place. Postgres usually adds a new column when a counter's unit changes, so tools that read the old column keep working.
objections.author_must_show: Why redefine dealloc in place instead of keeping it and adding a separate column for evicted entries?

critic.reasoning: Message #9 states that dealloc changes from eviction runs to evicted entries and asks for views, and no reviewer answered. The claim about usual Postgres practice has no support in the material, but the break for tools that read the column stands without it.

refuted.title: Renaming the pg_stat_statements wait event breaks existing monitoring
refuted.failure_scenario: A dashboard filters pg_stat_activity.wait_event = 'pg_stat_statements' to spot the eviction lock convoys. If the event is renamed pg_stat_statements_alloc, the filter matches nothing after upgrade. The dashboard reports no contention while the new events are present but not watched.
refuted.argument: Open item 1 in message #28 proposes the rename for symmetry and notes that tools watching the old name would need updating. The existing name also changes meaning, because it no longer covers eviction. A committer would likely ask whether symmetry is worth a silent break in tools that have used this name for years.
refuted.author_must_show: What does a user gain from the rename that keeping the existing pg_stat_statements name for entry creation would not give?

critic.reasoning: Message #28 raises the rename as an open question and states its cost to tools that watch the old name. Wait event names have changed between major versions before, and the eviction convoys that such a dashboard watches for are what the series removes.

refuted.title: Any role can fill query_text_memory and blank texts for all users
refuted.failure_scenario: An unprivileged role runs many distinct statements with long normalized texts, such as long IN lists or large generated queries, and fills the 4MB query_text_memory. New entries from other roles then show an empty query column. The DBA finds out only during an incident, when the needed statement has no text.
refuted.argument: With 0004, texts live only in capped shared memory, and the 4MB default allows about 800 bytes per entry at max = 5000. Today a large text file costs disk space, but every entry keeps its text. Message #28 says real query texts are larger than the benchmark texts, and nothing shown limits a single role's share or says when blank texts are filled in again. The backstop at twice max lets the same churn stop new entries from being tracked at all.
refuted.author_must_show: When one role's distinct long statements fill query_text_memory or reach the backstop, which statements from other roles lose their text or their entry, and how does a DBA detect it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1: the failure is the same empty query column at the cap. Upstream has no per-role limit either, so one role's churn can already evict other roles' entries, and message #28 reports the backstop is not reached with 0002.

refuted.title: Shared memory grows with a soft max and never shrinks
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator raises pg_stat_statements.max to 100000 with a reload during a churn incident, then lowers it back. The dshash keeps its peak size until restart. The backstop of twice max, or at most 20,000 more, is fixed in code, so the operator cannot bound the peak.
refuted.argument: The v4 documentation says the dynamic shared memory 'is not reclaimed when entries are deallocated', and v5 makes max a soft limit. PGC_SIGHUP invites exactly this raise-then-lower pattern, but nothing undoes the growth. Message #28 gives the backstop constants without saying how they were chosen.
refuted.author_must_show: What bounds the peak shared memory of pg_stat_statements after max is raised and lowered, and can an operator get it back without a restart?

critic.reasoning: The peak is bounded by the backstop derived from the max the operator set, and the documentation hunk states that memory is reused but not returned. Upstream allocates memory for max at server start and also needs a restart to shrink it, so this is not a regression.

refuted.title: Removing the query text file commits all users to capped in-memory texts
refuted.failure_scenario: A site with long ORM-generated queries upgrades and keeps the 4MB default query_text_memory. New entries show an empty query column, and monitoring tools that snapshot pg_stat_statements store statistics with no text. The site finds out when it is investigating a slow query.
refuted.argument: Message #28 states that 0004 is the goal, and also states that real query texts are much larger than the benchmark texts. Message #5 noted that large text files are common on customer systems. The author's point, that reads already need this memory, covers peak memory only. Once the file path is gone, a return to it is a new format change.
refuted.author_must_show: What default for query_text_memory keeps texts for real workloads with long queries, and what does a user see when the cap is reached?

precedents.title: Cancel problems of query to pg_stat_statements

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, with the same scenario and the same question to the author. P7 records a committer pointing toward in-memory texts, so it does not support this objection, and message #28 says 0003 can go in alone with the file kept.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: Entries move from the module's own file into the core pgstat stats file, and the final patch removes the query text file.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The series adds the own_hash kind option, pgstat_get_hash_for_kind() and a release-after-flush option to the pgstat API for extensions.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The series adds pg_stat_statements.query_text_memory and changes pg_stat_statements.max to PGC_SIGHUP with soft-limit semantics.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: pgstat gains a second reference-lifetime mode and a per-kind dshash that every later pgstat change must keep correct.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Counter updates run on every tracked statement; the author reports some low-client datapoints 1% to 4% slower than upstream.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: What happens to relation and other core stats at restart when the stats file holds pg_stat_statements entries but the module is no longer loaded?
In v5/v6, does pg_stat_statements.save = off still stop entries from being written and restored, and how do entries and query texts stay consistent after restart?
How does a user learn that query_text_memory is full, and which default keeps texts for workloads with long queries?
Which other stats kind would use the release-after-flush option, and which test fails if a later pgstat change breaks it?
Why redefine pg_stat_statements_info.dealloc in place instead of keeping it and adding a separate column for evicted entries?

committability.owner_note: Several pgstat infrastructure pieces from the series are already committed, so a committer who knows the cumulative statistics code is involved. No reviewer has replied to v5/v6 yet.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the pgstat API additions used by extensions, the stats file behaviour with a widely loaded custom kind, and changed meanings of pg_stat_statements.max and dealloc, for as long as the module ships.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted six versions over six months, split pieces into separate threads on request, and moved the entry through four CommitFests.

priority.reason: The gains appear from 32 vCPUs up and under query churn, in one of the most widely used contrib modules. The main patch is about 130 KiB and touches both pgstat core and pg_stat_statements, so review is costly, but the open points are fixable.

provisional_note: Without the code, the stats file reader's handling of an unregistered kind, the eviction and backstop logic, and the flush path cost at low client counts could not be checked. Message #28 is truncated, so some open items may already cover the questions above.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_stat_statements with plans (v02)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch extends pg_stat_statements to store a good plan and a bad plan for each normalized query, captured when execution time falls outside a configurable range around the usual time. Later versions use one GUC, pg_stat_statements.plan_track, plus a fence factor based on estimated quartiles, and one overloaded pg_stat_statements_plan_reset() function.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown messages, from March 2018, propose one row per plan or a separate plans view and coordination with other pg_stat_statements work. No author reply or closing message is shown.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_stat_statements with plans
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Simon Riggs, Peter Eisentraut, David Steele
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch extends pg_stat_statements to store one good and one bad execution plan per entry, with time and timestamp, in six new view columns. A plan is replaced when execution time falls below 0.9 or rises above 1.1 times the stored time, with GUCs for these factors, the plan format and a minimum update interval.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Simon Riggs and Peter Eisentraut objected to the fixed 10% threshold for good and bad plans and suggested a statistical deviation measure instead. Peter Eisentraut added that execution time can vary for reasons other than the plan, that cost numbers should be tracked, and that the design might hide the difference between generic and specific plans. David Steele noted the patch was large, had received little discussion, and was marked Returned with Feedback; the author said he had little time to work on it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The other problem is that this measures execution time, which can vary
for reasons other than plan.  I would have expected that the cost
numbers are tracked somehow.

precedents_retrieved.title: Sampling of queries in pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_stat_statements.sample_rate setting so pg_stat_statements records statistics for only a fraction of queries, which lowers its overhead under high load. Later versions moved the sampling check into pgss_enabled() and set the per-query sampling decision in pgss_post_parse_analyze().
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not say why the author withdrew the entry, one day after posting it. The only reservation came from Michael Paquier, who did not want to add sampling before studying the actual bottlenecks. He suggested moving pg_stat_statements into the central pgstats with the custom APIs, which would remove the query text file and shrink the hash key, but he did not plan that work for PG18.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: FWIW, I'm not eager to integrate this proposal without looking at this exact argument in depth.

precedents_retrieved.title: Sampling in pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a pg_stat_statements.sample_rate setting so that pg_stat_statements records statistics for only a random fraction of queries, to reduce spinlock contention on hot entries on large machines. The author briefly replaced it with an execution-time threshold (track_min_duration), then went back to random sampling.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it as Returned with Feedback, stating that the change was not a priority and that integrating pg_stat_statements with central pgstats was more important. Before that, the patch had been marked ready for committer, but no committer took it up. Alena Rybakina had objected that random sampling can drop the queries that matter.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since at the moment these changes are not a priority, and it's more important to address [0] for pg_stat_statements, I'm marking this patch as "Returned with Feedback".

precedents_retrieved.title: Sample values for pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pg_stat_statements store sample values for the constants and parameters of each normalized query, taken from its first execution and shown in new view columns. Settings switch collection on or off and limit the size of stored values.
precedents_retrieved.objection: After a version bump in pg_stat_statements the patch no longer applied, and the author did not post a rebased version, so the entry was closed after two months with no activity. Andres Freund's points were never settled in the thread: stored bind parameters could expose passwords to users who may read pg_stat_statements, and the query text file could grow large.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: As nothing has happened since, I'm marking this as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Planning counters in pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add planning counters to pg_stat_statements: a count of how many times a statement was planned and the total planning time, recorded through a planner hook alongside the existing execution counters. The patch passed the planning time to the executor through a new PlannedStmt field and had the planner hook bump the existing nesting level counter.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to the design: pgss_ExecutorEnd cleared a field in the cached PlannedStmt, which he said amounted to modifying the plan cache. He also questioned whether the planner hook should change nested_level, and he said the approach assumed a near one-to-one relationship between planner and executor calls that does not hold for cases such as prepared statements. He proposed having the planner hook record planning time with its own pgss_store() call. The author found that this needs the query text in the planner, which would mean changing function signatures, and returned the patch with feedback because he did not have time to rework it during the commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
What we have here is pgss_ExecutorEnd stomping on the plan cache.
I do *not* find that acceptable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Cancel problems of query to pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make pg_stat_statements queries cancellable by adding interrupt checks inside the read loop of qtext_load_file, which loads the query text file, and by cutting the read chunk size from 1GB to 32MB so the checks run more often. Because the function can run while pgss->lock is held, v2 only records that an interrupt is pending inside the loop and calls CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS after the loop ends and the lock is released.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andrey Borodin first noted that the lock held during the file read blocks interrupts anyway; v2 worked around that. Michael Paquier then rejected the patch as only a workaround for a larger problem: the on-disk PGSS query text file does not scale once it is large and entries turn over often. He pointed instead to a planned rework that would move pg_stat_statements onto the pgstats API as a custom stats kind, with the query texts held entirely in memory.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch is only a workaround for a larger problem: the PGSS text
file does not and will never scale once it reaches a large size and
once we have a high turnover rate of the PGSS entries due to different
query IDs.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve cursor handling in pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes pg_stat_statements so that DECLARE CURSOR statements are normalized, get a queryId and have their planning time tracked. Execution statistics are then counted under the DECLARE CURSOR entry instead of under FETCH, and CLOSE is no longer tracked.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Only the author's opening message is shown, with no replies, and the entry was withdrawn about four weeks later.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent records a reason that applies against this proposal. P7, P3 and P4 each name the move to a custom pgstats kind with in-memory texts as the preferred direction, and this series is that move. P9 and P12 have no recorded reason. The open questions about in-memory-only texts and the backstop belong to other angles.

The SQL-level surface stays small, and making pg_stat_statements.max PGC_SIGHUP is a widely wanted change. The objections above are about existing view columns, wait events and text availability that change under unchanged names.

Other persistent state looks acceptable. WAL is not touched. Standby behavior follows existing pgstat rules. pg_upgrade does not carry pg_stat files, so the old pg_stat_statements file format does not need to upgrade. The ABI changes affect only the master branch.

The remaining privilege aspects look unchanged: view access, reset functions, and the pid-signalling flush from v0 were dropped. Without the code I could not check whether the new info columns or wait events expose anything new.
Not applicable. The direction has committer support: message #17 and precedents P7, P3 and P4 favour moving pg_stat_statements to pgstats, so the objections above are about parts of the design.

No existing feature, setting or well-known extension removes the per-entry spinlock and the exclusive eviction lock that the thread measures. Raising pg_stat_statements.max needs a restart and does not touch hot-entry contention. The design reuses the core pgstat machinery instead of adding a second one. Earlier sampling and text-file workarounds [P3], [P4], [P7] were set aside in favour of this direction.

The material shows real, lasting demand. Message #1 cites a field complaint, several independent people back the goal (message #5: "Let's fix this for Postgres 20"), and the topic drew sessions at PGConf.dev and PGConf.EU. Rejections [P7], [P3] and [P4] each pointed to this rework as the preferred fix, and pg_stat_statements is one of the most widely used contrib modules.
